title: Rethinking GNNs and Missing Features
one_liner: A graph neural network must handle missing node data realistically, and simple baselines beat specialized tricks once you measure this fairly.
lead: In the real world, a graph (sensor networks have nodes as devices, edges connecting them) often has incomplete data—some readings are never collected. Graph neural networks are models that learn to answer questions about graphs. But testing them on standard benchmark data gives a false sense of their performance gaps, because the benchmark data is sparse and missing values are scattered at random. This paper shows that sparse data actually makes missing values harmless—so all methods appear equally good—and proposes fairer tests with dense, realistic data and missing patterns that match the real world.

paras: A graph neural network is a model trained to predict or classify parts of a graph. In real deployments (hospitals, power grids, sensor nets), data is often incomplete—some node measurements are simply missing. A naive approach: train on complete data, then at test time, replace missing values with zero or a default stand-in. This fails in practice because the missing pattern is not random; some features go missing together, and the model never learned what that means.

But the standard benchmarks (datasets widely used to compare models) hide this problem. They have two features that make missing data harmless: (1) each node has hundreds of features but only a few carry real information, and (2) the missing values are scattered uniformly at random. In this setup, losing a few scattered features loses almost no real signal—the useless noise vanishes. The result: every model reaches the same accuracy, because when nearly all the lost data is noise, no method can suffer much from its absence. Researchers cannot tell which approaches handle missing data better, because the test is not hard enough to separate good methods from bad.

callout.html: Standard benchmarks are too easy; they make missing data look harmless when it is not, so all methods appear equally good.

steps.text: Show mathematically that high sparsity shrinks how much real signal is lost when data goes missing.
Create datasets where each feature carries real information and there are many features, matching real deployments.
Design protocols where features go missing in correlated patterns, not uniformly random.
Train a straightforward graph model adapted to the graph domain with no special tricks.
Compare the baseline to specialized methods on the new benchmarks and real missingness patterns.

paras: The paper changes the test suite: instead of using sparse, randomly-missing benchmark data, it proposes dense datasets with missing patterns that cluster—entire feature groups go missing together, just as in real sensor nets. It also proposes a simple baseline: take a standard graph neural network and adapt it to missing values by learning a mask or imputation for each node, without complex architectural tricks.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: information loss from sparsity
hidden.name: information loss fraction
paras: The hidden quantity is how much real signal is actually lost when a feature is missing. In a sparse dataset (where most features are noise), losing one noisy feature loses almost no signal. In a dense dataset (where every feature carries information), losing one feature loses a lot of signal. This paper measures information loss by proving a theoretical bound: sparse data shrinks loss (so all methods reach the same accuracy), while dense data exposes the true cost (so methods that handle missing data well separate from those that do not).

The paper also operationalizes missingness: instead of assuming all features are equally likely to be missing (MCAR, missing completely at random), it considers structured missingness where features go missing in correlated blocks. This means the model must learn not just to handle missing data, but to infer whole feature groups from their neighbors.

heat.caption: Darker means more information is actually lost when data goes missing. Sparsity + random missingness (lower-left) hides the problem; dense data + structured missingness (upper-right) reveals it.

reads.html: Imagine two sensor nets: one with 1,000 mostly-useless measurements per node, one with 10 highly-informative measurements. If a single random sensor breaks in each, the first net barely notices (1 in 1,000 of the measurements is gone, but most were noise anyway), but the second net loses 10% of its real signal. The first benchmark is like the first net, and the real world is like the second.

The paper proves that information loss is bounded by sparsity: high-dimensional sparse features limit how much real information is lost when values are missing at random. This implies benchmark data designed with high sparsity will show all methods reaching similar accuracy, because the missing data does not hurt much, so differences between methods do not show up.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: dense data exposes what matters
paras: The core mechanism is simple: if a feature is noise, losing it does not affect accuracy. If a feature is signal, losing it hurts accuracy. Sparse benchmarks have mostly noise, so missing data causes little accuracy drop, and any method reaches high scores. Dense benchmarks have mostly signal, so missing data causes large accuracy drops, and only methods that handle missing data well stay accurate. The theory proves this: for sparse (high-dimensional but low information) data, the information-theoretic bound on loss is tiny, so all methods end up close to the same accuracy. For dense (low-dimensional but high information) data, the bound is large, and methods that ignore missing patterns lose more accuracy than methods that learn to fill in the gaps.

The paper also introduces structured missingness: instead of assuming each feature is independently missing with probability p (random), it assumes entire feature groups go missing together. This is more realistic (if a sensor on a node fails, all its readings disappear, not just one). When missingness is structured, a model that just pads missing values with zeros or learns a single imputation misses the opportunity to infer an entire group from context. A method that acknowledges the block structure (e.g., by learning to fill in groups coherently) will do better. A simple baseline adapted to the graph domain (learning how to weight available neighbors' features as substitutes) can match or beat specialized architectures on these harder benchmarks.

stages.s: Sparse benchmark: mostly noise. Dense benchmark: mostly signal.
Information loss: tiny from sparse, large from dense.
Model performance gap: hidden in sparse, visible in dense.

math.words: information loss is at most the product of the number of features and the sparsity level, divided by total feature count
symbols: fraction of signal information lost when a feature goes missing
how many features on each node
fraction of features that carry no useful signal

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Sparse benchmark: 1,000 features per node, 950 are noise, 50 are signal. Sparsity = 950/1000 = 0.95.
InfoLoss <= (1000 * 0.95) / 1000 = 0.95. When one random feature is missing, on average 0.95 of the lost information was noise anyway.
Dense benchmark: 10 features per node, 2 are noise, 8 are signal. Sparsity = 2/10 = 0.2.
InfoLoss <= (10 * 0.2) / 10 = 0.2. When one random feature is missing, only 0.2 of the loss was noise; 0.8 was signal. Loss bites much harder.

math.note: In sparse data, missing a feature rarely loses real signal; in dense data, every missing feature hurts accuracy. This bound explains why benchmarks with high sparsity hide the performance gap between good and poor methods.

bars.h2: Performance on old vs new benchmarks

charts.title: Old sparse benchmark (MCAR)
charts.note: All methods perform similarly; the sparse, randomly-missing data does not stress-test them.

charts.title: New dense benchmark (structured missingness)
charts.note: On fair tests with dense features and realistic missingness, specialized methods and a simple graph-adapted baseline both do much better than naive padding. The naive baseline loses 25% accuracy because it does not adapt to the graph structure; both better methods recover most of it by learning from neighbors.

items.b: Sparse data still hides poor methods.
items.html: If your benchmark stays high-dimensional and sparse, even a method that guesses at missing values will reach high accuracy, because the missing data does not hurt much—the sparsity is doing the work, not the method. You need dense features that actually carry signal to expose which methods truly handle missing data well.

items.b: Assuming random missingness when the real pattern is structured.
items.html: If the real world has entire sensor types failing (structured), but you test only with random gaps, your model will not learn to fill in the gaps coherently. It will be blind to block-level patterns.

items.b: Using a method that learns one global imputation.
items.html: A method that replaces all missing values with the dataset mean does worse on dense, structured-miss data, because different nodes and feature blocks need different imputations. A simple neighborhood-aware baseline beats it.

Test on dense data with realistic missingness patterns. Use a method that learns how to fill in different nodes or feature blocks differently, because not every node or feature type needs the same imputation. A simple baseline adapted to the graph structure (so a node's neighbors help fill its gaps) works well because neighbors carry redundant information and can often substitute for missing features.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic graph with 20 nodes, each with 10 dense features (no noise). Create two test conditions: (1) remove 30% of features uniformly at random (the old benchmark), (2) remove 30% by removing entire feature blocks (the new benchmark, more realistic). Train three models: a naive baseline that pads missing values with zero, a specialized architecture, and a simple graph-adapted baseline that learns to reconstruct missing features from available neighbors. Measure accuracy on a node-classification task.
demo.closing: The demo should show that all methods lose less than 5% accuracy on the old random-missingness test (all look good), but on the new block-missingness test, the naive baseline drops 25%+ while the simple graph-adapted baseline stays within 10% of full data. This proves dense, realistic missingness is necessary to separate good methods from bad.
